questions.question_text: Given 2^x * 4^y = 1/(2*sqrt(2)), express y as a function of x. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text: B1: Writes a correct equation in powers of 2 only, e.g. 2^x * 2^(2y) = 2^(-3/2) (or an equivalent equation using logarithms, e.g. x*log2 + 2y*log2 = log(1/(2*sqrt(2)))). M1: Complete process of using correct index laws (or log laws) on a correct equation to obtain y written as a function of x. A1: y = -x/2 - 3/4 (o.e., e.g. y = -(1/4)(2x+3)). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
The speed of a small jet aircraft was measured every 5 seconds, starting from the time it turned onto a runway, until the time when it left the ground. The results are given in the table below with the time in seconds and the speed in m/s.
Time (s): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
Speed (m/s): 2, 5, 10, 18, 28, 42
Using all of this information,
(a) estimate the length of runway used by the jet to take off. (3 marks)
Given that the jet accelerated smoothly in these 25 seconds,
(b) explain whether your answer to part (a) is an underestimate or an overestimate of the length of runway used by the jet to take off. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Uses an allowable method to estimate the area under the speed-time curve (e.g. the trapezium rule, a uniform-acceleration equation, or summing rectangles). M1: Correct trapezium rule method with h=5 (condone a slip on one of the speeds): Area = (5/2)*[2 + 42 + 2*(5+10+18+28)]. A1: 415 (m) (units not required, but final A0 if incorrect units are given). (3 marks)
(b) B1ft: Overestimate, with a relevant explanation, e.g. the top of the trapezia lie above the curve / the curve is convex / the acceleration (gradient) is continually increasing, so the area of the trapezia is greater than the area under the curve. (Depends on having obtained an answer to (a) using a trapezium-rule-type method; if a 'sum of rectangles lying below the curve' method was used instead in (a), then 'underestimate' with the explanation 'all the rectangles lie below the curve' is accepted.) (1 mark)

questions.question_text:
Figure 1 shows a sector AOB of a circle with centre O, radius 5 cm and angle AOB = 40°. The attempt of a student to find the area of the sector is shown below.
Area of sector = (1/2)*r^2*theta = (1/2)*5^2*40 = 500 cm^2
(a) Explain the error made by this student. (1 mark)
(b) Write out a correct solution. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Explains that the sector-area formula (1/2)*r^2*theta is only valid when theta is measured in radians; the student has substituted theta = 40 in degrees instead of converting to radians. (1 mark)
(b) M1: Correct application of the sector-area formula using theta converted to radians (theta = 40*pi/180 = 2*pi/9), or equivalently using the degrees version of the formula, (theta/360)*pi*r^2. A1: Area = 25*pi/9 cm^2, or awrt 8.73 cm^2 (units may be ignored for this mark). (2 marks)

questions.question_text: Figure 2 shows a sketch of the curve C1 with parametric equations x = 10*cos(t), y = 4*sqrt(2)*sin(t), 0 <= t < 2*pi, which meets the circle C2 with equation x^2 + y^2 = 66 at four distinct points, as shown in Figure 2. Given that one of these points, S, lies in the 4th quadrant, find the Cartesian coordinates of S. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Begins to solve the problem by applying a complete strategy, e.g. substituting the parametric equations for C1 into the Cartesian equation for C2 to give an equation in one variable (t) only (alternative valid strategies: convert C1 to Cartesian form using sin^2(t)+cos^2(t)=1 and combine with C2; or write C2 in parametric form and combine parametrically). M1: Uses sin^2(t)+cos^2(t)=1 to reduce the equation to sin^2(t) only, or cos^2(t) only (or, in an x/y-only approach, to an equation in x^2 only or y^2 only; or, using double-angle formulae, to an equation in cos(2t) only). A1: Correct resulting equation, e.g. (10cos t)^2 + (4*sqrt(2)*sin t)^2 = 66 leading to 100 - 68*sin^2(t) = 66, i.e. sin^2(t) = 1/2. dM1: Rearranges to find sin(t) (or cos(t), or x^2/y^2, or cos(2t)), where the result lies in the valid range; dependent on both previous M marks. M1: Substitutes the solution back into the relevant original equation(s) to obtain the value of the x-coordinate and the corresponding y-coordinate (note: these may not yet be in the correct quadrant). A1: Selects the coordinates lying in the 4th quadrant: S = (5*sqrt(2), -4), i.e. S = (awrt 7.07, -4). (6 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 3 shows a sketch of the curve with equation y = sqrt(x). The point P(x, y) lies on the curve. The rectangle, shown shaded on Figure 3, has height y and width (delta x). Calculate
lim_{delta x -> 0} Sum_{x=4}^{9} sqrt(x) * (delta x)
(3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text: B1: States that the limit equals the definite integral, Integral from 4 to 9 of sqrt(x) dx (with or without the 'dx'). M1: Integrates sqrt(x) = x^(1/2) to give k*x^(3/2), k not equal to 0. A1: Correct value: [(2/3)*x^(3/2)] from 4 to 9 = (2/3)*27 - (2/3)*8 = 38/3, i.e. 12 and 2/3, or awrt 12.7. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 4 shows a sketch of the graph of y = g(x), where
g(x) = (x-2)^2 + 1, for x <= 2
g(x) = 4x - 7, for x > 2
(a) Find the value of gg(0). (2 marks)
(b) Find all values of x for which g(x) > 28. (4 marks)
The function h is defined by
h(x) = (x-2)^2 + 1, x <= 2
(c) Explain why h has an inverse but g does not. (1 mark)
(d) Solve the equation
h^{-1}(x) = -1/2
(3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Uses a complete method to find gg(0), e.g. substitutes x=0 into (0-2)^2+1 to get 5, then substitutes this result into the relevant branch of g. A1: gg(0) = g(5) = 4(5)-7 = 13. (2 marks)
(b) M1: Solves (x-2)^2+1 = 28 (or 4x-7 = 28) to find a critical value. A1: At least one correct critical value is found: x = 2 - 3*sqrt(3) (awrt -3.20) or x = 35/4 (= 8.75). M1: Solves both (x-2)^2+1 = 28 (relevant to the branch x<=2) and 4x-7 = 28 (relevant to the branch x>2). A1: Correct final answer: x < 2 - 3*sqrt(3), x > 35/4 (i.e. x > 8.75) (set notation is acceptable). (4 marks)
(c) B1: h is one-one (so has an inverse); g is many-one (so does not have an inverse). A correct explanation conveying both underlined points is needed, e.g. 'h is one-one and g is many-one'. (1 mark)
(d) M1: Finds h^{-1}(x) = 2 - sqrt(x-1) (or, equivalently, uses the fact that if h^{-1}(x) = -1/2 then x = h(-1/2), without needing h^{-1} explicitly). M1: Sets 2 - sqrt(x-1) = -1/2 (or x = h(-1/2)) and attempts to solve for x. A1: x = 7.25 only, cso. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
A small factory makes bars of soap. On any day, the total cost to the factory, £y, of making x bars of soap is modelled to be the sum of two separate elements: a fixed cost, and a cost that is proportional to the number of bars of soap that are made that day.
(a) Write down a general equation linking y with x, for this model. (1 mark)
The bars of soap are sold for £2 each. On a day when 800 bars of soap are made and sold, the factory makes a profit of £500. On a day when 300 bars of soap are made and sold, the factory makes a loss of £80. Using the above information,
(b) show that y = 0.84x + 428 (3 marks)
(c) With reference to the model, interpret the significance of the value 0.84 in the equation. (1 mark)
Assuming that each bar of soap is sold on the day it is made,
(d) find the least number of bars of soap that must be made on any given day for the factory to make a profit that day. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: y = kx + c, where k > 0 and c > 0 are constants (must be seen in part (a); work here cannot be recovered in (b) or (c)). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Translates the problem into the model by finding the total cost on each day: for x=800, y = 2(800)-500 = 1100; for x=300, y = 2(300)-(-80) = 680 (i.e. revenue minus profit, or revenue plus loss). dM1: Applies the two points (800,1100) and (300,680) to form and solve two simultaneous equations for k and c (e.g. k = (1100-680)/(800-300) = 0.84, then substitutes back to find c = 428). A1*: Correct proof with no errors, leading to y = 0.84x + 428 (the answer must be stated in part (b)). (3 marks)
(c) B1: 0.84 (in £s) represents the cost of making each extra bar of soap (the direct/marginal cost of making a bar of soap). Do not allow 'profit per bar' or 'selling price per bar'. (1 mark)
(d) M1: Uses the model, with revenue 2n and cost 0.84n+428, to construct an inequality/equation for profit (2n > 0.84n + 428) and rearranges for n. A1: 369 (bars) - the least whole number of bars for which a profit is made (decimal answers not accepted). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
(i) Find the value of
Sum_{r=4}^{infinity} 20*(1/2)^r
(3 marks)
(ii) Show that
Sum_{n=1}^{48} log_5((n+2)/(n+1)) = 2
(3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(i) M1: Applies a/(1-r) with their common ratio r (where -1 < r < 1) and their value of a (e.g. a = 20*(1/2)^4 = 1.25). M1: Finds the infinite sum using a completely correct strategy (e.g. sum-to-infinity of the whole series minus the sum of the first three terms, or directly a/(1-r)). A1: 2.5 (o.e.). (3 marks)
(ii) M1: Some evidence of applying the subtraction law of logs and beginning to solve the problem, e.g. writing (or combining) at least three terms of the sum, including either the first two terms and the last term, or the first term and the last two terms (this reveals the telescoping pattern). M1: Uses the subtraction law of logs to write the sum as (log_5 3 + log_5 4 + ... + log_5 50) - (log_5 2 + log_5 3 + ... + log_5 49), or an equivalent telescoping form. A1*: Correct proof leading to log_5(50/2) = log_5(25) = 2. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
A research engineer is testing the effectiveness of the braking system of a car when it is driven in wet conditions. The engineer measures and records the braking distance, d metres, when the brakes are applied from a speed of V km/h. Graphs of d against V and log10(d) against log10(V) were plotted. Figure 5 shows the graph of d against V, with a data point (30, 20) marked on the curve. Figure 6 shows the graph of log10(d) against log10(V), a straight line with vertical-axis intercept -1.77.
(a) Explain how Figure 6 would lead the engineer to believe that the braking distance should be modelled by the formula
d = k*V^n, where k and n are constants,
with k = awrt 0.017 (3 marks)
Using the information given in Figure 5, with k = 0.017,
(b) find a complete equation for the model, giving the value of n to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
Sean is driving this car at 60 km/h in wet conditions when he notices a large puddle in the road 100 m ahead. It takes him 0.8 seconds to react before applying the brakes.
(c) Use your formula to find out if Sean will be able to stop before reaching the puddle. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Writes log10(d) = log10(k) + n*log10(V) (or log10(d) = m*log10(V) + c, or log10(d) = m*log10(V) - 1.77), seen or used as part of the argument. A1: Alludes to d = k*V^n and gives a full explanation by comparing the result with a linear model Y = MX + C (i.e. a straight-line log-log graph implies a power-law relationship between d and V). B1*: k = 10^(-1.77) = awrt 0.017, linked together with the -1.77 intercept in the same part of the question. (3 marks)
(b) M1: Applies V=30 and d=20 to the model (correct way round), i.e. 20 = k*(30)^n or log10(20) = log10(k) + n*log10(30). M1: Applies (V,d) = (30,20) and applies logarithms correctly, rearranging to find n. A1: n = awrt 2.08, giving d = 0.017*V^2.08 (or log10(d) = -1.77 + 2.08*log10(V)). (3 marks)
(c) M1: Applies V=60 to the model to find the braking distance d (d = 0.017*(60)^2.08, awrt 84.9). M1: Uses the model in a correct problem-solving process, either adding a 'thinking distance' (0.8 * velocity in m/s = awrt 13.3 m) to the braking distance to find the total stopping distance, or subtracting the thinking distance from 100 m and comparing with d. A1ft: Correct comparison and conclusion, e.g. 13.3 + 84.9 = 98.25 < 100, so Sean stops in time (ft on their k, n provided a sensible model results). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 7 shows a sketch of triangle OAB. The point C is such that OC = 2*OA. The point M is the midpoint of AB. The straight line through C and M cuts OB at the point N. Given OA = a and OB = b,
(a) Find CM in terms of a and b (2 marks)
(b) Show that ON = (2 - (3/2)*lambda)*a + (1/2)*lambda*b, where lambda is a scalar constant. (2 marks)
(c) Hence prove that ON : NB = 2 : 1 (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Valid attempt to find CM using a combination of the known vectors a and b, e.g. CM = CA + AM = -a + (1/2)(b-a), or CM = CB + BM = (-2a+b) + (1/2)(a-b). A1: Correct simplified answer: CM = -(3/2)*a + (1/2)*b. (2 marks)
(b) M1: Uses ON = OC + lambda*CM. A1*: Correct proof, substituting OC = 2a and CM = -(3/2)a + (1/2)b, to obtain ON = (2 - (3/2)*lambda)*a + (1/2)*lambda*b. (2 marks)
(c) M1: Deduces (since N lies on OB, so ON has no component of a) that 2 - (3/2)*lambda = 0, and solves to find lambda = 4/3. A1*: Substitutes back to get ON = (2/3)*b, so NB = OB - ON = b - (2/3)*b = (1/3)*b, hence ON : NB = (2/3)*b : (1/3)*b = 2 : 1. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 8 shows a sketch of the curve C with equation y = x^x, x > 0.
(a) Find, by firstly taking logarithms, the x coordinate of the turning point of C. (Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.) (5 marks)
The point P(alpha, 2) lies on C.
(b) Show that 1.5 < alpha < 1.6 (2 marks)
A possible iteration formula that could be used in an attempt to find alpha is
x_{n+1} = 2*x_n^(1 - x_n)
Using this formula with x_1 = 1.5,
(c) find x_4 to 3 decimal places, (2 marks)
(d) describe the long-term behaviour of x_n (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Takes logs of both sides: ln(y) = x*ln(x) (condone use of log base 10, or writing y = e^(x*ln x)). M1: Differentiates implicitly: (1/y)*(dy/dx) = 1 + ln(x) (or, using y = e^(x ln x), dy/dx = (ln x + x/x)*e^(x ln x)). A1: Correct differentiated equation, e.g. (1/y)*(dy/dx) = 1 + ln(x), or dy/dx = x^x*(1 + ln x). M1: Sets 1 + ln(x) = 0 and rearranges to make ln(x) = k (k a constant, k < 0), then x = ... . A1: x = e^(-1), or awrt 0.368 only (with no other solutions given). (5 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts both 1.5^1.5 (= awrt 1.8) and 1.6^1.6 (= awrt 2.1), with at least one result correct to 1 dp. A1: 1.8... < 2 and 2.1... > 2, and since C is continuous, there is a sign change between x=1.5 and x=1.6, so 1.5 < alpha < 1.6. (2 marks)
(c) M1: Attempts x_{n+1} = 2*x_n^(1-x_n) at least once with x_1 = 1.5 (can be implied by 2*(1.5)^(1-1.5) = awrt 1.63). A1: x_4 = 1.673 (3 dp), cao (via x_2 = 1.63299..., x_3 = 1.46626..., x_4 = 1.67313...). (2 marks)
(d) B1: States that the sequence oscillates / is periodic / non-convergent / divergent / fluctuates / alternates (e.g. 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, ...). B1: States that it oscillates specifically between 1 and 2, or is periodic with period 2. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Prove
cos(3*theta)/sin(theta) + sin(3*theta)/cos(theta) ≡ 2*cot(2*theta), theta ≠ (90n)°, n ∈ ℤ (4 marks)
(b) Hence solve, for 90° <= theta <= 180°, the equation
cos(3*theta)/sin(theta) + sin(3*theta)/cos(theta) = 4
giving any solutions to one decimal place. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Correct valid method forming a common denominator of sin(theta)*cos(theta), i.e. [cos(3theta)*cos(theta) - sin(3theta)*sin(theta)] / [sin(theta)*cos(theta)] (or, equivalently, starting from the RHS and expanding cos(2theta) as cos(3theta)*cos(theta) + sin(3theta)*sin(theta)). A1: Proceeds to show that the numerator simplifies to cos(3theta+theta) = cos(4theta), using the compound-angle formula for cosine. dM1: Applies a correct sin(2theta) = 2*sin(theta)*cos(theta) to the denominator, dependent on the previous M mark. A1*: Correct proof: cos(4theta) / [(1/2)*sin(2theta)] = 2*cot(2theta). (4 marks)
(b) M1: Evidence of applying cot(2theta) = 1/tan(2theta) to rewrite the equation as tan(2theta) = 1/2 (o.e., k not equal to 0). dM1: Rearranges to give tan(2theta) = k, k not equal to 0, and applies arctan(k); dependent on the previous M mark. A1: Uses 90 <= theta <= 180 to deduce the only solution theta = awrt 103.3 (1 dp), with no other (extraneous) solutions given. (3 marks)

questions.question_text: A manufacturer produces a storage tank modelled as a hollow circular cylinder, closed at one end, with a hemispherical shell at the other end (Figure 9). The walls are assumed to have negligible thickness. The cylinder has radius r metres and height h metres; the hemisphere has radius r metres. The volume of the tank is 6 m^3. [A sphere of radius r has volume (4/3)*pi*r^3 and surface area 4*pi*r^2.] (a) Show that, according to the model, the surface area of the tank, in m^2, is given by A = 12/r + (5/3)*pi*r^2. (4 marks) The manufacturer needs to minimise the surface area of the tank. (b) Use calculus to find the radius of the tank for which the surface area is a minimum. (4 marks) (c) Calculate the minimum surface area of the tank, giving your answer to the nearest integer. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: correct expression for the volume of the tank in terms of r and h (cylinder + hemisphere). M1: complete process of substituting their h (in terms of r) into an expression for the surface area of the form A = alpha*r^2 + beta*r*h. A1: correct simplified or unsimplified surface area expression, e.g. A = 2*pi*r^2 + 2*pi*r*h + (2/3)*pi*r^2, using h from the volume constraint. A1*: proceeds, with rigorous and careful reasoning, to A = 12/r + (5/3)*pi*r^2 (given answer). (4 marks)
(b) M1: uses the model and differentiates r^-1 and r^2 terms correctly in form/sign. A1: correct dA/dr = -12/r^2 + (10/3)*pi*r. M1: sets their dA/dr = 0 and rearranges to r^3 = k for some constant k. A1: r = awrt 1.05 (m), or exact form. (4 marks)
(c) M1: substitutes their r back into the expression for A. A1: minimum surface area = awrt (nearest integer) m^2, consistent with their r. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Use the substitution u = 4 - sqrt(h) to show that
Integral of dh/(4 - sqrt(h)) = -8*ln|4 - sqrt(h)| - 2*sqrt(h) + k
where k is a constant (6 marks)
A team of scientists is studying a species of slow growing tree. The rate of change in height of a tree in this species is modelled by the differential equation
dh/dt = [t^0.25 * (4 - sqrt(h))] / 20
where h is the height in metres and t is the time, measured in years, after the tree is planted.
(b) Find, according to the model, the range in heights of trees in this species. (2 marks)
One of these trees is one metre high when it is first planted. According to the model,
(c) calculate the time this tree would take to reach a height of 12 metres, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (7 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: States or uses du/dh = -1/(2*sqrt(h)) (equivalently, since u=4-sqrt(h) gives sqrt(h)=4-u and h=(4-u)^2, dh/du = -2*(4-u)). M1: Complete method for applying u=4-sqrt(h) to dh/(4-sqrt(h)) to give an expression of the form k*(4-u)/u {du}, k not equal to 0. M1: Proceeds to obtain an integral of the form A/u + B {du}; A, B not equal to 0. A1: Integrates to give -8*ln|u| + 2u {+c} (with or without a constant of integration). A1*: Substitutes u=4-sqrt(h) back into the integrated result and completes the proof to obtain the printed result -8*ln|4-sqrt(h)| - 2*sqrt(h) + k, combining the constants correctly. (6 marks)
(b) M1: Uses the context of the model, understanding that the tree keeps growing until dh/dt = 0, i.e. 4 - sqrt(h) = 0. A1: Deduces 0 <= h < 16 (or h <= 16, or an equivalent statement giving 16 as the limiting height). (2 marks)
(c) B1: Separates the variables correctly: dh/(4-sqrt(h)) = (t^0.25 / 20) dt (dh and dt in the correct positions; can be implied by later working). M1: Integrates t^0.25 to give (4/5)*t^1.25. A1: Correct integration, e.g. -8*ln|4-sqrt(h)| - 2*sqrt(h) = (4/5)*t^1.25 {+ constant}. M1: Some evidence of applying both t=0, h=1 to their model (containing a constant of integration) to find that constant, OR applying limits h=1 to h=12 and t=0 to T and subtracting. dM1: Complete process of finding the constant of integration (or applying both sets of limits), then applying h=12 to give an equation in t only; dependent on the previous M mark. M1: Rearranges their equation to make t^1.25 = ..., then t = ... (t>0), using a correct method. A1: t = awrt 75.2 (years) (3 sf). (7 marks)
